title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Evaluate Source Credibility During Deep Web Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, making them vulnerable to misinformation, outdated sources, and low-quality content. When LRMs autonomously gather information for research reports, uncritical incorporation of unreliable sources can silently degrade output quality in ways that are hard to detect. Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, extending the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with an explicit Credibility Assessment Module (CAM). During reasoning, before incorporating extracted web content, the model executes structured credibility checks: (1) source authority scoring via domain reputation signals and citation metadata, (2) cross-source consistency verification by querying multiple independent sources for contested claims, and (3) temporal validity assessment flagging potentially outdated information. We train the credibility assessment behavior using a contrastive DPO approach, constructing preference pairs where reliable-source-grounded responses are preferred over equivalent responses using low-credibility sources, even when factual content appears similar. Training data is constructed by injecting known misinformation alongside correct sources into research tasks. Experiments: We evaluate on GAIA, GPQA, and HLE benchmarks augmented with adversarial web environments containing planted misinformation. We also introduce CredResearch-Bench, a new benchmark of 500 research tasks with ground-truth source reliability annotations, measuring both factual accuracy and source quality simultaneously.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Vision-Grounded Web Reasoning with Image and Chart Understanding
description:
Problem: Current deep research agents like WebThinker operate primarily on textual web content, yet a substantial portion of scientific and technical knowledge is encoded in figures, charts, diagrams, and tables embedded in web pages and PDFs. This gap limits research quality on domains like materials science, biology, and finance where visual evidence is critical.

Proposed Method: We extend the WebThinker framework with a Multimodal Deep Web Explorer that intercepts and processes visual content during web navigation. The agent learns to (1) identify when visual content is relevant to the current reasoning chain, (2) invoke a vision-language model to extract structured information from charts/figures/tables, and (3) integrate visual evidence into the think-search-draft loop. We introduce a visual-grounded citation mechanism that links report claims to specific image regions. Training uses iterative online DPO with multimodal preference pairs, where rewards combine textual accuracy with visual grounding quality assessed by an automated judge.

Experiments: We evaluate on: (1) existing benchmarks augmented with visual-answer subsets (GAIA-Visual, HLE-Visual), (2) a new benchmark MMResearchBench covering 500 queries requiring chart/figure synthesis across scientific domains, and (3) Glaive report quality with human evaluation of figure-backed claims. Baselines include WebThinker, GPT-4o with browsing, and Gemini Deep Research.

title: TrustThinker: Calibrated Uncertainty Quantification for Deep Research Agents via Source-Aware Confidence Estimation
description: Problem: Deep research agents like WebThinker synthesize information from diverse web sources, but provide no principled uncertainty estimates. Users cannot distinguish high-confidence synthesized claims backed by multiple authoritative sources from speculative extrapolations, limiting deployment in high-stakes domains (medical, legal, scientific). Proposed Method: We introduce TrustThinker, which augments the Think-Search-and-Draft pipeline with source-aware confidence estimation. At each reasoning step, we train a lightweight calibration head that tracks: (1) source authority scores (citation count, domain credibility), (2) cross-source consistency signals (agreement across retrieved documents), and (3) reasoning chain depth (how many inferential hops removed from retrieved evidence). We fine-tune using a calibration objective combining Expected Calibration Error (ECE) minimization with DPO, generating preference pairs where confident claims are grounded in high-agreement authoritative sources versus uncertain ones. During report drafting, claims are annotated with calibrated confidence intervals and provenance trails. Planned Experiments: Evaluate calibration quality on GPQA, GAIA, and HLE using ECE and reliability diagrams. Conduct human evaluations measuring trust and decision-making quality on medical literature synthesis tasks. Compare against baseline uncertainty methods (temperature scaling, verbalized confidence). Ablate contribution of each uncertainty signal component. Target: well-calibrated agents that explicitly communicate epistemic boundaries.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Cross-Modal Scientific Discovery with Vision-Augmented Web Exploration
description: Problem: Current deep research agents like WebThinker operate primarily on textual web content, yet a significant portion of scientific knowledge is encoded in figures, charts, tables, and diagrams. When reasoning over complex scientific tasks (e.g., interpreting experimental results, understanding molecular structures, analyzing clinical imaging data), an agent that ignores visual content is fundamentally limited. Proposed Method: We extend the WebThinker framework with a Vision-Augmented Deep Web Explorer (VA-DWE) that integrates a multimodal LRM backbone capable of extracting and reasoning over both textual and visual content from web pages. When the agent encounters knowledge gaps, it can not only extract text but also parse figures, interpret plots, and query image-specific content. We introduce a Chart-and-Figure Reasoning module that converts visual scientific artifacts into structured representations (e.g., data tables, captions, relationships) that feed back into the reasoning chain. Training uses an extended iterative DPO pipeline with multimodal preference pairs derived from scientific figure QA benchmarks. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) ScienceQA and ChartQA for multimodal scientific reasoning, (2) a newly curated benchmark of research report generation tasks requiring figure interpretation, and (3) GPQA/GAIA subsets with visual dependencies, comparing against text-only WebThinker and proprietary multimodal agents.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Heterogeneous Scientific Data through Vision-Augmented Think-Search-and-Draft
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents operate primarily on textual web content, but real-world scientific research requires synthesizing heterogeneous sources including figures, tables, charts, microscopy images, and experimental plots. Current LRM-based agents lack the ability to extract structured knowledge from visual scientific artifacts encountered during web navigation, limiting their utility for domains like biology, chemistry, and materials science.

Proposed Method: We extend the WebThinker framework with a Multimodal Deep Web Explorer that integrates a vision-language model (VLM) component alongside the text-based navigator. When the agent encounters web pages containing scientific figures, PDFs with embedded charts, or image-rich content, it invokes specialized visual reasoning tools: (1) a chart/table extractor that converts visual data into structured numerical representations, (2) a figure captioning module that generates semantically rich descriptions for inclusion in reasoning chains, and (3) a cross-modal consistency checker that flags contradictions between textual claims and visual evidence. Training uses multimodal DPO with preference pairs distinguishing reports that correctly interpret visual data from those ignoring or misinterpreting it.

Experiments: Evaluate on (1) ScienceQA and ChartQA requiring visual reasoning, (2) a new benchmark of 500 biomedical research questions requiring figure interpretation, (3) scientific report generation quality assessed by domain experts comparing text-only vs. multimodal variants, and (4) ablations on each visual tool component.

title: CollabThinker: Multi-Agent Deep Research via Specialized Role Decomposition and Consensus-Driven Synthesis
description:
Problem: WebThinker uses a single LRM to handle all research subtasks—query formulation, web navigation, evidence extraction, and report drafting—creating bottlenecks when tasks require simultaneously broad exploration and deep domain expertise. A single agent must serially pursue diverse research threads, limiting coverage and introducing confirmation bias in evidence synthesis.

Proposed Method: CollabThinker decomposes deep research into specialized roles assigned to distinct LRM instances: (1) a Strategist agent that decomposes the research question into sub-queries and maintains a global knowledge graph, (2) multiple parallel Explorer agents that each conduct WebThinker-style deep web exploration on assigned sub-queries, and (3) a Synthesizer agent that resolves contradictions across Explorer outputs via structured debate and drafts the final report. Agents communicate via a shared structured scratchpad. We train the multi-agent system using a multi-agent variant of iterative DPO, where reward signals account for both individual agent quality and collective report coherence.

Experiments: Evaluate on GAIA, GPQA, HLE, and Glaive benchmarks. Ablations isolate contributions of role specialization, parallelism, and debate-based synthesis. We measure factual accuracy, coverage breadth, inter-source contradiction resolution, and report completeness versus WebThinker and single-agent baselines. Human evaluation assesses report depth and coherence on open-ended scientific topics.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Evaluate Source Credibility During Deep Research
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, making them vulnerable to misinformation, outdated content, and low-quality sources. When synthesizing information across diverse web pages, LRMs lack mechanisms to assess source reliability, leading to hallucinated or factually incorrect research outputs.

Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft paradigm with an explicit Credibility Assessment Module (CAM). CAM operates at two levels: (1) source-level scoring using signals like domain authority, publication recency, citation counts, and author credentials extracted via lightweight classifiers; (2) cross-source consistency checking via embedding-based contradiction detection across retrieved passages. We train the model using a modified DPO objective that rewards outputs citing high-credibility, internally consistent sources over plausible-sounding but unreliable ones. A new synthetic dataset is constructed by injecting adversarial misinformation into web retrieval pipelines to create preference pairs.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) existing benchmarks (GPQA, GAIA, HLE) augmented with injected misinformation; (2) a new MisInfoResearch benchmark we construct with deliberately contaminated web corpora; (3) factual precision/recall of generated reports judged by expert annotators. Ablations isolate contributions of source-level scoring vs. consistency checking vs. credibility-aware DPO training.

title: VerifyThinker: Grounded Claim Verification for Deep Research Agents via Source-Aware Reasoning Chains
description: Problem: Deep research agents like WebThinker can synthesize information from multiple web sources, but they lack mechanisms to verify factual accuracy and detect contradictions across retrieved documents. This leads to hallucinated or outdated claims in generated reports, particularly on rapidly evolving scientific topics where sources conflict. Proposed Method: We introduce VerifyThinker, which augments the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with an explicit Claim-Verification loop. After drafting each report section, a dedicated verification module extracts atomic factual claims, retrieves targeted evidence for each claim, and runs a cross-source consistency checker that scores agreement/disagreement across sources. Contradicted or low-confidence claims trigger additional targeted searches. We train the verification module using contrastive DPO: preferred traces are those that correctly flag and resolve contradictions, while rejected traces accept conflicting evidence uncritically. Source provenance is embedded in reasoning chains as structured citations, enabling fine-grained attribution. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) existing WebThinker benchmarks (GPQA, GAIA) measuring factual accuracy; (2) a newly constructed ConflictingWeb benchmark with deliberately planted contradictory sources; (3) scientific misinformation detection tasks. We compare against WebThinker baseline, RAG-with-verification pipelines, and proprietary systems, measuring claim-level precision, contradiction detection recall, and human-rated report trustworthiness.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Evaluate Source Credibility During Deep Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat retrieved web content as uniformly trustworthy, but real-world web sources vary dramatically in credibility, recency, and bias. This creates a critical failure mode where agents synthesize misinformation or low-quality sources into research reports without flagging uncertainty, undermining reliability in high-stakes domains like medical, legal, or scientific research. Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft pipeline with an inline Source Credibility Assessment (SCA) module. During reasoning, when the agent retrieves content, it triggers a credibility sub-process that evaluates: (1) domain authority signals (citation counts, institutional affiliation, publication venue), (2) cross-source consistency via automatic claim triangulation across multiple retrieved documents, and (3) temporal reliability (publication date vs. claim validity). We train the SCA module using RL with a reward signal that penalizes reports citing low-credibility or conflicting sources without appropriate hedging language. Training uses synthetic adversarial web corpora mixing reliable and unreliable sources. Experiments: We construct a new benchmark, WebCredEval, with 500 research tasks where ground-truth answers require discriminating between reliable and unreliable sources. We evaluate claim accuracy, appropriate uncertainty expression, and source citation quality against WebThinker, Perplexity, and GPT-4o with search, measuring factual precision and calibration.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Evaluate Source Credibility During Deep Web Research
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, yet real-world web sources vary dramatically in reliability, recency, and bias. This creates a critical vulnerability where LRMs may synthesize misinformation into research reports without any credibility assessment, particularly harmful in scientific, medical, and political domains.

Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft pipeline with an explicit Source Credibility Evaluation (SCE) module. During reasoning, before incorporating retrieved content, the model executes credibility checks: (1) domain authority scoring via cross-referencing citation graphs and institutional affiliations, (2) cross-source consistency verification by querying multiple independent sources and detecting factual contradictions, and (3) temporal reliability assessment flagging outdated information. We train the SCE module using RL with a novel reward signal that penalizes reports containing verifiable factual errors sourced from low-credibility pages, using GPT-4o as a fact-checking judge. Training data includes synthetically injected misinformation at varying subtlety levels.

Experiments: We evaluate on GPQA, GAIA, and HLE benchmarks augmented with adversarially inserted unreliable sources in the retrieval environment. Additional evaluation on a new MisinfoResearch benchmark covering medical/scientific claims. Metrics include factual accuracy, credibility-weighted citation rates, and human expert ratings of report trustworthiness, comparing against WebThinker and Search-o1 baselines.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Visual and Tabular Web Content
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents primarily process textual web content, yet a substantial portion of web-based knowledge is encoded in images, charts, figures, and structured tables. This limitation prevents LRMs from fully synthesizing scientific papers with figures, financial reports with charts, or Wikipedia infoboxes with complex tables during deep research tasks.

Proposed Method: We introduce MultiModalThinker, extending the WebThinker framework with a multimodal perception layer that enables the reasoning agent to extract, interpret, and integrate visual and tabular content during its Think-Search-and-Draft cycle. Specifically, we add: (1) a Chart/Figure Interpreter module that applies vision-language models to parse graphs, diagrams, and scientific figures into structured textual summaries; (2) a Table Reasoning module that performs programmatic analysis over HTML/PDF tables using tool-augmented code execution; and (3) a multimodal context aggregator that fuses visual evidence with textual snippets before feeding into the reasoning chain. We train the agent using iterative DPO with preference pairs that reward accurate cross-modal synthesis.

Experiments: We evaluate on multimodal-heavy benchmarks including ChartQA, FinQA, SciMMIR, and a new MultiModal-GAIA split we construct by filtering GAIA tasks requiring visual web content. Ablations isolate contributions of each modality module, and human evaluation measures report coherence and factual grounding.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Knowledge Staleness and Temporal Uncertainty During Web Research
description:
Problem: Web-augmented reasoning models like WebThinker retrieve information dynamically but treat all retrieved content as equally reliable regardless of temporal context. This is problematic for time-sensitive domains (medical guidelines, legal regulations, financial data, scientific consensus) where outdated information can cause confident but incorrect conclusions. Current systems lack mechanisms to detect knowledge staleness, reconcile conflicting temporal signals across sources, or express calibrated uncertainty about time-dependent facts.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, extending the think-search-draft paradigm with explicit temporal reasoning capabilities. Key components: (1) Temporal Provenance Tracking — each retrieved snippet is annotated with publication date and recency score, propagated through the reasoning chain; (2) Temporal Conflict Resolver — when sources contradict across time, the model explicitly reasons about which is authoritative and why; (3) Staleness-Aware Confidence Calibration — the model outputs explicit temporal uncertainty estimates alongside answers; (4) RL training using DPO with temporal-consistency reward signals, penalizing answers that ignore recency signals or fail to flag time-sensitive uncertainty.

Experiments: Evaluate on a new benchmark TempKnow comprising 500 questions where ground truth has changed over time (medical, legal, tech domains). Compare against WebThinker, Perplexity, and GPT-4o with search on temporal accuracy, calibration (ECE), and staleness detection F1. Ablate each temporal component.

title: SourceThinker: Credibility-Aware Deep Research with Adversarial Web Content Robustness
description: Problem: Current deep research agents like WebThinker treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, making them vulnerable to misinformation, outdated sources, SEO-poisoned pages, and adversarial content injection. When synthesizing research reports from diverse web sources, LRMs may unknowingly incorporate fabricated statistics, biased narratives, or deliberately misleading information, undermining report reliability in high-stakes domains like medicine, law, and science. Proposed Method: We introduce SourceThinker, extending the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with a Credibility-Aware Synthesis module. During the reasoning process, the model maintains a dynamic source credibility graph tracking provenance, cross-source consistency, and citation networks. We augment the DPO training with adversarial examples containing planted misinformation, training the model to prefer responses that cross-validate claims across multiple independent sources and explicitly flag uncertain or conflicting information. A learned credibility scorer evaluates domain authority, publication recency, and cross-reference density, integrated directly into the RL reward signal. Planned Experiments: (1) Construct a benchmark of research queries with deliberately poisoned web environments using controlled misinformation injection; (2) Evaluate factual accuracy on medical (PubMedQA), legal, and scientific domains; (3) Compare against WebThinker and retrieval-augmented baselines on claim verification rates and hallucination metrics; (4) Human evaluation of report trustworthiness and appropriate uncertainty expression.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Validity During Deep Research
description: Problem: When LRMs like WebThinker gather information from the web, they treat all retrieved content as equally valid regardless of temporal context. This leads to critical failures when reasoning about rapidly evolving topics—models may synthesize contradictory information from different time periods, rely on outdated facts, or fail to recognize when their internal knowledge conflicts with newer web content due to training cutoffs. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, which augments the deep research pipeline with explicit temporal reasoning capabilities. The system adds: (1) a Temporal Metadata Extractor that tags retrieved web content with publication dates and recency scores, (2) a Temporal Conflict Detector that identifies when retrieved sources contradict each other or the model's priors across time, and (3) a Freshness-Aware Synthesis strategy that conditions report generation on explicit temporal reasoning chains (e.g., 'As of [date], X was true, but by [date], Y superseded it'). Training uses DPO with preference pairs where temporally-aware responses are preferred over temporally-naive ones. Experiments: We construct a TemporalQA benchmark spanning science, finance, and geopolitics with ground-truth temporal validity windows. We evaluate on fact accuracy stratified by information age, temporal conflict resolution rate, and downstream report quality on time-sensitive Glaive tasks, comparing against WebThinker and RAG baselines.

title: CiteThinker: Grounded Scientific Report Generation with Verifiable Citation Chains via Reasoning-Integrated Retrieval
description:
Problem: While WebThinker enables LRMs to synthesize web information into research reports, a critical unsolved challenge is factual grounding and citation verification — generated reports often contain hallucinated or misattributed citations, undermining scientific trustworthiness. Current systems lack mechanisms to ensure every factual claim is traceable to a verified source retrieved during reasoning.

Proposed Method: CiteThinker extends the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with a Citation Chain Module (CCM) that operates during the reasoning process. For each factual assertion drafted, the model maintains a structured claim-evidence graph linking statements to specific retrieved passages with provenance metadata (URL, publication date, author). We introduce a Citation Verification Reward in RL training: beyond answer correctness, the model receives rewards for citation precision (retrieved passages actually support claims) and citation recall (all verifiable claims are cited). We use automated fact-checking via a secondary verifier LLM to score citation quality during iterative DPO training.

Experiments: (1) Scientific report quality on Glaive with human evaluation of citation accuracy; (2) A new CiteBench benchmark with 500 annotated claims requiring verifiable sourcing; (3) Ablations on CCM vs. no-citation baseline; (4) Cross-domain evaluation on medical and legal report generation where citation correctness is safety-critical; (5) Human expert evaluation of report trustworthiness scores.

title: VerifyThinker: Grounded Credibility Assessment During Deep Research via Source-Aware Reasoning
description: Problem: Deep research agents like WebThinker retrieve and synthesize web information, but treat all sources equally, making them vulnerable to misinformation, outdated content, and low-credibility sources. This undermines trustworthiness of generated reports, especially for high-stakes domains like medical or scientific research. Proposed Method: We introduce VerifyThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft pipeline with an explicit credibility verification layer. For each retrieved web snippet, the model maintains a structured source metadata graph tracking: domain authority scores, publication recency, citation networks, and cross-source consistency. We introduce a 'Verify' action alongside Search/Navigate/Draft, allowing the model to explicitly cross-reference claims across multiple independent sources before incorporating them. We train this verification behavior using a contrastive DPO approach: positive trajectories involve successful claim triangulation before drafting, while negative trajectories accept single-source claims uncritically. Ground-truth credibility labels are derived from fact-checking datasets (FEVER, VitaminC) augmented with domain-expert annotations. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) existing WebThinker benchmarks measuring factual accuracy under deliberately injected misinformation in retrieved pages, (2) a new MedResearch benchmark requiring synthesis of clinical evidence, and (3) human expert ratings of report trustworthiness. We measure hallucination rate, source diversity, and claim verification coverage as novel metrics.

title: SourceThinker: Credibility-Aware Deep Research with Adversarial Web Content Robustness
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, making them vulnerable to misinformation, SEO-poisoned pages, and adversarial content injection. This is critical for high-stakes domains like medical, legal, or scientific research where a single misleading source can corrupt entire reasoning chains and final reports. Proposed Method: We introduce SourceThinker, which augments the WebThinker framework with a credibility-aware retrieval and synthesis pipeline. First, we train a lightweight source credibility scorer using domain authority signals, cross-reference consistency, and temporal recency. Second, we introduce a contrastive claim verification module that detects conflicting claims across sources and triggers targeted re-search to resolve contradictions. Third, we add adversarial robustness training by synthetically injecting poisoned web pages during RL-based DPO training, forcing the model to discount and flag unreliable content. Finally, the report drafting stage includes uncertainty quantification, annotating claims by source reliability. Experiments: We construct a new benchmark, AdversarialResearch-Bench, containing 500 research queries with deliberately seeded misinformation across web corpora. We evaluate source-citation accuracy, hallucination rates, and report factuality against WebThinker, GPT-4o search, and Perplexity Pro. We also test on GAIA and GPQA under adversarial conditions to measure robustness degradation.

title: SourceThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Critically Evaluate and Cite Web Sources During Deep Research
description:
Problem: While WebThinker enables LRMs to retrieve and synthesize web information, it treats all retrieved content as equally trustworthy. Real-world web research demands critical source evaluation—distinguishing credible from unreliable sources, detecting contradictions across sources, and producing verifiable citations. Current deep research agents lack mechanisms for epistemic source assessment, leading to confident reports built on dubious information.

Proposed Method: We introduce SourceThinker, extending the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with an explicit Credibility-Weighted Synthesis layer. The model maintains a dynamic source reliability graph tracking domain authority, publication recency, cross-source consistency, and citation networks. During reasoning, we add a 'Verify' action alongside Search/Navigate that triggers contradiction detection between retrieved passages. We train a source-scoring auxiliary head jointly with the main reasoning model using RL rewards that penalize reports citing low-credibility or contradictory sources. Fine-tuning uses DPO on contrastive pairs where one response appropriately hedges uncertain claims with source quality caveats while the other does not.

Experiments: (1) Factual accuracy on FEVER and ClaimBuster benchmarks measuring hallucination reduction; (2) Citation quality evaluation on scientific report generation using automated credibility metrics; (3) Human evaluation of report trustworthiness versus WebThinker baseline; (4) Adversarial robustness when injecting misinformation into retrieved documents. We expect SourceThinker to significantly reduce confident errors while maintaining task performance.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Uncertainty During Web Research
description: Problem: Web-augmented reasoning systems like WebThinker retrieve information dynamically but treat all retrieved content as equally trustworthy regardless of temporal validity. This leads to reasoning errors when synthesizing contradictory information across time (e.g., outdated statistics, superseded scientific findings, evolving events), a critical failure mode for knowledge-intensive tasks. Proposed Method: TemporalThinker augments the deep research pipeline with three components: (1) a Temporal Credibility Estimator that tags retrieved web content with freshness scores based on publication dates, domain decay rates, and topic volatility; (2) a Temporal Conflict Resolver that explicitly prompts the reasoning model to identify, articulate, and reconcile contradictions between time-stamped sources during the thinking process; and (3) a temporally-aware DPO training scheme where preference pairs are constructed by comparing responses that correctly handle temporal conflicts versus those that naively merge contradictory information. Training signals come from automatically generated temporal conflict scenarios using Wikipedia revision histories. Experiments: Evaluate on a newly constructed TemporalQA benchmark with 1,500 questions requiring synthesis of time-sensitive web information across science, finance, and policy domains. Also evaluate on existing GAIA and HLE benchmarks stratified by temporal sensitivity. Baselines include WebThinker, vanilla RAG, and GPT-4o with search.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Heterogeneous Scientific Data Sources
description:
Problem: Current deep research agents like WebThinker excel at extracting textual information from web pages but fail to reason over heterogeneous scientific data modalities—tables, figures, charts, plots, and equations—that are critical for tasks like literature synthesis, experimental result comparison, and hypothesis generation in STEM domains. This bottleneck severely limits utility for real scientific research workflows.

Proposed Method: We propose MultiModalThinker, which augments the WebThinker framework with a Multimodal Evidence Extraction module capable of (1) parsing and reasoning over figures/charts from PDFs and web pages using a vision-language model, (2) extracting structured data from tables via specialized table-parsing tools, and (3) interpreting mathematical equations using a symbolic reasoning component. We introduce a Think-Search-See-and-Draft strategy where the agent dynamically decides whether to invoke text, visual, or symbolic extraction tools based on content type. Training uses iterative DPO with multimodal preference pairs constructed by comparing agent outputs against ground-truth scientific answers requiring visual evidence.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) ScienceQA and CharXiv benchmarks requiring chart/figure understanding, (2) a new Scientific Synthesis benchmark requiring cross-modal evidence aggregation from arXiv papers, and (3) Glaive report generation with multimodal content quality scoring. Ablations isolate contributions of each modality module.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Cross-Modal Evidence Synthesis from Scientific Figures, Tables, and Text
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat web content as plain text, ignoring rich multimodal information in scientific papers—figures, charts, tables, and diagrams—that often contain critical evidence not captured in text abstracts or HTML. This severely limits the quality of AI-generated research reports in technical domains.

Proposed Method: We extend the WebThinker framework with a multimodal evidence extraction layer that, upon retrieving a scientific webpage or PDF, employs a vision-language model to parse embedded figures and tables into structured semantic representations (captions, numerical claims, trend descriptions). A Cross-Modal Fusion module reconciles potentially conflicting claims across text, figures, and tables using structured evidence cards. We train a multimodal DPO strategy where preference pairs contrast reports backed by multimodal vs. text-only evidence, scored by domain expert annotation and automated factuality metrics.

Experiments: (1) Benchmark on ScienceQA, ChartQA, and a new MultiModalResearch benchmark requiring synthesis across figure+text pairs from arXiv papers. (2) Scientific report generation evaluated on figure-grounded factual accuracy via GPT-4V judge. (3) Ablations comparing text-only retrieval, figure-only, and fused approaches. (4) Human evaluation of report completeness and visual evidence utilization. We expect 10-15% gains on figure-grounded question answering and measurably richer generated reports.

title: SourceThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Critically Evaluate Web Source Reliability During Deep Research
description:
Problem: While WebThinker enables LRMs to autonomously gather web information, it treats all retrieved content with equal trust. In practice, web sources vary enormously in credibility—misinformation, outdated data, and biased sources can silently corrupt reasoning chains and final research reports without the model recognizing the contamination.

Proposed Method: We introduce SourceThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft pipeline with an explicit Source Credibility Assessment (SCA) module. During reasoning, whenever the model retrieves web content, it invokes a lightweight credibility scorer that estimates source reliability along multiple axes: domain authority, publication recency, cross-source corroboration, and claim verifiability. We fine-tune the LRM using RL-based DPO where reward signals explicitly penalize reports that cite low-credibility sources or contain factual contradictions between sources. The model learns to express calibrated uncertainty, seek corroborating evidence, and flag contested claims inline within drafts.

Experiments: (1) We construct a contaminated-web benchmark by injecting synthetic misinformation into retrieval corpora and measure report factual accuracy under adversarial conditions. (2) We evaluate on existing benchmarks (GAIA, GPQA, HLE) measuring both final accuracy and citation quality. (3) Human evaluation of generated research reports assessing hallucination rates and appropriate uncertainty expression. Baselines include WebThinker, vanilla RAG systems, and human researchers.

title: CiteThinker: Grounded Scientific Literature Synthesis with Verifiable Citation Chains in Deep Research Agents
description:
Problem: While WebThinker enables LRMs to gather web information during reasoning, scientific research tasks demand rigorous attribution—every factual claim must be traceable to specific passages in peer-reviewed sources. Current deep research agents produce fluent reports but hallucinate citations or misattribute claims, making them unreliable for academic use.

Proposed Method: CiteThinker extends the Think-Search-Draft paradigm with a Citation Grounding Module (CGM) that operates at sentence granularity. During drafting, the model explicitly tags each claim with a retrieval query, fetches candidate passages from academic sources (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, PubMed APIs), scores passage-claim entailment using a lightweight NLI verifier, and inserts verified inline citations. We introduce Citation-Aware DPO, where preference pairs are constructed by contrasting outputs with verified vs. unverified citation chains, rewarding the model for grounded claims over fluent-but-hallucinated ones. A citation consistency reward is added to the RL objective to penalize contradictory sourcing across report sections.

Experiments: (1) Citation precision/recall on SciReview-Bench—a new benchmark of 500 human-written survey sections with gold citations; (2) Factual accuracy evaluated via automated claim extraction + verification; (3) Ablations on CGM components and DPO variants; (4) Human evaluation of report coherence vs. grounding tradeoffs. Baselines include WebThinker, GPT-4o with retrieval, and Perplexity AI.

title: CiteVerifier: Grounding Deep Research Agents with Real-Time Citation Integrity Verification via Self-Correcting Retrieval Chains
description:
Problem: Deep research agents like WebThinker generate comprehensive reports by synthesizing web information, but they frequently produce hallucinated or misattributed citations—claiming sources support claims they don't actually contain. This undermines scientific credibility and trustworthiness of AI-generated reports, a critical gap for real-world deployment.

Proposed Method: We introduce CiteVerifier, a post-retrieval verification layer integrated into the Think-Search-and-Draft pipeline. After each draft segment is written with citations, CiteVerifier (1) re-fetches the cited URLs, (2) uses a lightweight entailment model to verify whether the cited content actually supports the drafted claim, and (3) triggers a self-correcting retrieval chain when verification fails—either finding alternative supporting sources or flagging the claim for revision. We train the verification-correction loop using RL with a composite reward combining task-answer correctness (from WebThinker's existing setup) and a citation fidelity score measuring entailment precision over sampled claim-source pairs.

Experiments: We evaluate on (1) scientific report generation (Glaive benchmark) with human expert annotation of citation accuracy, (2) GAIA and GPQA for downstream QA correctness, and (3) a new CitationBench dataset we construct by scraping fact-checkable claims from Wikipedia. Ablations isolate the verification module's contribution versus baseline WebThinker, measuring hallucination rate reduction and report faithfulness scores.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Detect and Resolve Conflicting Web Evidence During Deep Research
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents assume retrieved web information is consistent and trustworthy. In practice, web sources frequently contain contradictory facts, outdated claims, or misinformation, and current agents lack principled mechanisms to detect and reconcile such conflicts during reasoning and report generation. This can lead to hallucinated syntheses or uncritical adoption of incorrect information.

Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, which extends the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with an explicit Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) module. title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Vision-Intensive Scientific Domains via Interleaved Visual Reasoning and Web Exploration

title: TemporalThinker: Training Large Reasoning Models to Detect and Resolve Knowledge Staleness During Deep Research

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Visual Evidence Synthesis Across Scientific Literature

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Vision-Intensive Scientific Domains via Interleaved Image-Text Reasoning
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents operate primarily in text space, but many knowledge-intensive scientific tasks (e.g., medical diagnosis, materials science, astronomical discovery) require synthesizing information from charts, microscopy images, spectra, and figures embedded in papers and websites. Current LRMs cannot effectively extract or reason over visual evidence during web exploration, limiting their applicability in vision-critical research domains. Proposed Method: We introduce MultiModalThinker, a multimodal deep research agent that extends the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm to interleaved image-text reasoning. The system adds a Visual Evidence Extractor module that detects, crops, and encodes salient figures from retrieved web pages and PDFs using a vision-language backbone. A multimodal working memory stores retrieved text snippets alongside visual embeddings with provenance metadata. During drafting, the agent can cite and reason over figures directly. We train the system using RL-based iterative DPO with multimodal preference pairs, rewarding responses that correctly integrate visual evidence versus text-only answers. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) adapted GPQA questions requiring figure interpretation, (2) a new benchmark MultiModal-GAIA with vision-dependent subtasks, (3) medical case report generation (PubMed-cases), and (4) materials science synthesis tasks, comparing against WebThinker+GPT-4V and Gemini Deep Research baselines.

title: CiteThinker: Grounded Scientific Literature Synthesis with Verifiable Citation Chains via Reasoning-Augmented Retrieval
description: Problem: While WebThinker enables deep web research, scientific writing demands not just information retrieval but verifiable, attribution-grounded synthesis where every claim traces to specific evidence in peer-reviewed literature. Current LRM-based agents hallucinate citations or lose provenance during long reasoning chains, making them unreliable for academic use cases. Proposed Method: CiteThinker extends the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with a Citation Ledger mechanism that maintains a structured evidence graph throughout the reasoning process. Each retrieved passage is stored with its DOI, page, and quote span; reasoning steps explicitly reference ledger entries; and draft sentences are prohibited from making factual claims without a ledger pointer. We introduce a Claim-Citation Consistency reward trained via iterative DPO, incentivizing the model to prefer responses where every factual assertion is anchored to a verifiable source. A semantic deduplication module merges redundant evidence nodes to prevent context bloat. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) SciReviewBench—a new benchmark of 500 expert-written survey paragraphs requiring citation recall/precision, (2) existing Glaive report generation, and (3) a human study measuring hallucinated citation rate. Ablations test Citation Ledger vs. inline citations, and reward ablations isolate the contribution of citation consistency training.

title: VerifyThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Assess Source Credibility During Deep Web Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally trustworthy, but real-world web sources vary dramatically in reliability, recency, and potential bias. This leads to research reports that may confidently synthesize misinformation or contradictory claims without flagging uncertainty. Proposed Method: We introduce VerifyThinker, which augments the Think-Search-and-Draft pipeline with an explicit Credibility Assessment Module (CAM). During reasoning, before integrating any retrieved content, the model performs inline source verification: checking publication date, author credentials, cross-referencing claims across multiple independent sources, and detecting contradictions. We encode credibility signals as structured metadata tokens injected into the reasoning context. Training uses a novel Credibility-Aware DPO objective where preference pairs are constructed by contrasting reports that correctly identify unreliable sources versus those that naively incorporate them, using a curated benchmark of web pages with known ground-truth reliability labels. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on GAIA and GPQA with adversarially injected misinformation sources; (2) Introduce a new benchmark, WebCredEval, containing 500 research tasks where planted low-credibility pages contradict correct answers; (3) Human evaluation of final reports on scientific topics for factual accuracy and appropriate uncertainty expression; (4) Ablations on CAM components to isolate credibility signal contributions.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Uncertainty During Web Research
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web information as equally reliable regardless of temporal context. This causes critical failures when reasoning about rapidly evolving topics (e.g., scientific findings, geopolitical events, technology benchmarks) where outdated information can silently corrupt conclusions. LRMs lack explicit mechanisms to reason about *when* information was produced, whether it remains valid, and how to reconcile conflicting claims from different time periods.

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, extending the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm with a Temporal Credibility Assessment (TCA) module. TCA automatically tags retrieved documents with freshness scores, detects temporal contradictions between sources, and injects structured temporal metadata into the reasoning chain (e.g., '[SOURCE: 2023-04, POSSIBLY_OUTDATED]'). We add a temporal consistency reward to the DPO training objective, penalizing outputs that cite stale evidence when fresher sources are available, or that fail to acknowledge temporal uncertainty when sources conflict across time.

Experiments: (1) Construct a benchmark of 500 time-sensitive queries with ground-truth answers that changed over 2022-2025; (2) Evaluate temporal reasoning accuracy on GAIA, HLE subsets filtered for time-sensitive questions; (3) Human evaluation of generated reports for appropriate uncertainty hedging; (4) Ablations on TCA components and reward weighting. Baseline comparisons include vanilla WebThinker, GPT-4o with search, and Perplexity.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Uncertainty During Deep Research
description:
Problem: When LRMs like WebThinker retrieve web information, they treat all retrieved content as equally reliable regardless of publication date or temporal relevance. This leads to systematic errors on tasks requiring up-to-date knowledge, where older pages may contradict newer ones, or where the model must reason about whether information is stale. Current systems lack explicit mechanisms to detect, represent, and resolve temporal conflicts across retrieved sources.

Proposed Method: We augment the WebThinker framework with a Temporal Consistency Module (TCM) that (1) extracts and normalizes publication timestamps from retrieved pages, (2) constructs a temporal evidence graph representing conflicting claims across time, and (3) introduces a 'temporal uncertainty token' into the reasoning chain that forces the model to explicitly deliberate about information freshness before committing to an answer. We train this using RL-based DPO with a modified reward function that penalizes outdated conclusions when fresher contradicting evidence was available in the retrieved context.

Experiments: We construct a new benchmark, TemporalQA-Web, containing 1,500 questions where correct answers changed after a known cutoff date. We evaluate on GAIA, our new benchmark, and a modified HLE subset, measuring both accuracy and calibration of temporal uncertainty expressions. We compare against WebThinker baseline, RAG with recency ranking, and proprietary systems.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Visual Evidence Synthesis in Scientific Literature
description:
Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents primarily process textual web content, yet a substantial portion of scientific knowledge is encoded in figures, charts, tables, and diagrams embedded in papers and technical documents. Current agents cannot reason over visual evidence, limiting their utility for rigorous scientific research tasks requiring cross-modal synthesis.

Proposed Method: We extend the WebThinker framework with a Multimodal Deep Explorer (MDE) module that enables LRMs to (1) detect and extract visual elements from crawled web pages and PDF documents, (2) invoke a vision-language model (e.g., fine-tuned Qwen2-VL) to generate structured captions and numerical summaries from figures, and (3) maintain a unified evidence store interleaving text and visual summaries. We train the agent using iterative online DPO where rewards account for both textual accuracy and faithful visual evidence citation, using GPT-4o as a judge for multimodal faithfulness.

Experiments: (1) Scientific QA requiring chart interpretation (ChartQA, FigureQA, SciMMIR benchmarks). (2) Multimodal research report generation evaluated on Glaive extended with figure-referencing rubrics. (3) Ablation of text-only vs. multimodal evidence retrieval. (4) Human evaluation of report completeness and visual grounding. We expect substantial gains on visually-intensive scientific tasks over text-only WebThinker baselines.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Conflicts During Deep Research
description: Problem: Web-augmented reasoning models like WebThinker retrieve information from diverse sources with varying publication dates, but lack explicit mechanisms to detect temporal conflicts (e.g., outdated statistics, superseded findings) or reason about when retrieved facts were valid. This causes silent errors in knowledge-intensive tasks where temporal grounding matters critically. Proposed Method: TemporalThinker augments the deep research pipeline with three components: (1) a Temporal Metadata Extractor that annotates each retrieved chunk with publication timestamps and identifies time-sensitive claims; (2) a Conflict Detection Module that flags contradictions between sources attributable to temporal drift versus genuine disagreement; and (3) a Temporal Reasoning Chain that forces the model to explicitly reason about claim validity windows before incorporating evidence into answers or reports. Training uses a temporal-aware DPO variant where preference pairs are constructed by contrasting responses that correctly resolve temporal conflicts against those that naively aggregate outdated information. Experiments: Evaluate on (1) a new TemporalQA benchmark constructed from Wikipedia revision histories and fact-change databases; (2) existing GPQA and GAIA subsets requiring recent factual knowledge; (3) scientific report generation where statistics change over time. Baselines include WebThinker, Perplexity, and Gemini Deep Research. Metrics include temporal accuracy, conflict resolution rate, and report factuality scores.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Evaluate Source Credibility During Deep Web Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents treat all retrieved web content as equally reliable, making them vulnerable to misinformation, outdated information, and low-quality sources. When reasoning models autonomously gather web information, they may anchor on authoritative-sounding but factually incorrect content, compounding errors across long reasoning chains. Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, which augments the WebThinker framework with an integrated Source Credibility Assessment (SCA) module that operates within the reasoning loop. The SCA module assigns dynamic trust scores to retrieved content based on: (1) domain authority signals, (2) cross-source consistency verification via triangulation across multiple retrieved pages, (3) temporal validity checking against publication dates, and (4) citation network analysis for scientific claims. We train the model using a contrastive DPO objective where positive examples use high-credibility sources leading to correct answers, and negative examples use plausible-but-misleading sources. The model learns to explicitly reason about source reliability before incorporating information. Experiments: We construct a new benchmark, WebMisinfo-QA, containing questions where top search results include seductive misinformation alongside correct sources. We evaluate on existing benchmarks (GPQA, GAIA, HLE) with adversarially injected low-quality pages, measuring answer accuracy, source selection quality, and calibration of expressed uncertainty.

We construct a training dataset by crawling scientific claims paired with high/low quality supporting sources and use iterative DPO to train the model to preferentially cite credible sources, explicitly flag conflicting evidence, and hedge claims appropriately. Planned Experiments: (1) Factual accuracy on ClaimBuster and FactBench benchmarks; (2) Source quality metrics on generated reports evaluated by domain experts; (3) Robustness testing with injected misinformation; (4) Ablations on credibility graph components; (5) Human evaluation of appropriate epistemic hedging in final reports compared to WebThinker baseline.

title: TemporalThinker: Training Large Reasoning Models to Detect and Resolve Knowledge Staleness During Deep Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents assume all retrieved web content is equally trustworthy and temporally relevant. However, LRMs frequently encounter conflicting information across sources with different publication dates, causing reasoning chains to silently incorporate outdated facts—particularly critical in fast-moving domains like medicine, policy, and technology. No existing work explicitly trains models to detect temporal inconsistencies between internal parametric knowledge and retrieved content, nor to reason about which source to trust based on recency and authority. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, which extends the Think-Search-Draft paradigm with a Temporal Consistency Verification (TCV) module. TCV prompts the model to explicitly timestamp-tag retrieved claims, flag conflicts between sources, and emit structured uncertainty markers when recency cannot be established. We construct a synthetic training dataset by injecting deliberately outdated documents into retrieval corpora for factual QA tasks, then apply iterative online DPO where preferred trajectories correctly identify and resolve temporal conflicts while dispreferred ones ignore them. We also introduce a contrastive retrieval reward that penalizes citing stale sources when fresher alternatives exist. Experiments: We evaluate on a new benchmark, StaleFactQA, covering 2,000 questions across medicine, law, and AI research where ground truth changed post-2023. We compare against WebThinker, Perplexity, and GPT-4o Search on accuracy, staleness-error rate, and source recency metrics.

description:

Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, which augments the think-search-draft pipeline with explicit temporal consistency reasoning. Key components: (1) a Temporal Metadata Extractor that tags each retrieved chunk with publication date and estimated staleness score; (2) a Temporal Conflict Detector that identifies contradictions between sources from different time periods during the reasoning chain; (3) a Recency-Weighted Synthesis module that adjusts source credibility dynamically based on temporal relevance to the query; (4) RL training via DPO with temporal consistency rewards, penalizing reports that cite outdated information when newer sources contradict them.

Experiments: We construct a new benchmark, TemporalQA, comprising 500 questions requiring multi-hop reasoning across time-sensitive web documents (medical guidelines, tech specs, geopolitical facts). We evaluate against WebThinker and baseline RAG systems on temporal accuracy, contradiction rate in generated reports, and human-judged coherence. Ablations isolate each temporal component's contribution.

title: CriticalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Detect and Recover from Misinformation During Deep Web Research
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents assume retrieved web content is trustworthy, but real-world web searches frequently surface misinformation, outdated facts, contradictory sources, and SEO-manipulated content. When LRMs uncritically incorporate such information into long reasoning chains, errors propagate and compound, ultimately corrupting research reports with confident-sounding falsehoods. Proposed Method: We introduce CriticalThinker, extending the Think-Search-Draft paradigm with an explicit Verify-and-Reconcile module. When the agent retrieves information, a lightweight credibility scorer (trained on a curated dataset of reliable vs. unreliable sources) flags suspicious content. The LRM then triggers adversarial cross-checking: deliberately searching for contradicting evidence and reasoning explicitly about source conflicts before committing information to the draft. We train this skeptical behavior using iterative DPO where preference pairs contrast reports that blindly adopt misleading sources versus reports that detect and correct them. The training signal comes from a semi-automated pipeline that injects synthetic misinformation into retrieved documents and rewards recovery. Experiments: We evaluate on augmented versions of GAIA and HLE with injected misinformation, a new benchmark MisInfoResearch-500 comprising tasks with known web misinformation, and factual accuracy metrics on Glaive report generation, comparing against WebThinker and RAG-based baselines.

description:

We train the model using DPO on preference pairs where temporally-aware resolutions are preferred over temporally-naive ones, using synthetic conflict injection as data augmentation.

Experiments: We create TempConflictQA, a benchmark of 500 questions requiring temporal arbitration across 3+ conflicting web sources. We evaluate on existing benchmarks (GAIA, GPQA) augmented with temporal noise injection, measuring factual accuracy, temporal consistency scores, and citation recency appropriateness. Ablations isolate the TCM's contribution versus base WebThinker.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Uncertainty During Deep Research

(2) Evaluate on GAIA and HLE subsets filtered for temporally-sensitive questions. (3) Ablate freshness decay modeling, uncertainty token insertion, and temporal DPO individually. (4) Human evaluation of calibration in generated research reports on rapidly-evolving topics.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Reliability During Web Research
description: Problem: When LRMs like WebThinker retrieve web information, they treat all sources as equally reliable regardless of publication date, recency requirements, or temporal consistency across sources. We train this with RL-based DPO using preference pairs where temporally-aware answers are preferred over stale-information answers. Experiments: We create a new benchmark TempResearch-QA with 500 questions requiring temporal reasoning across domains (medicine, finance, technology, geopolitics). We evaluate on existing benchmarks (GAIA, GPQA subsets with temporal sensitivity), measuring answer accuracy, temporal consistency scores, and hallucination rates on time-sensitive claims, comparing against WebThinker and GPT-4o with search.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Consistency During Deep Research
description:

We train the model using DPO on preference pairs where temporally-consistent reports are preferred over those with anachronistic synthesis.

title: MultiModalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Vision-Grounded Web Reasoning with Chart, Table, and Image Understanding

Planned Experiments: (1) Construct a new benchmark, MultiModal-Research-QA, sampling 500 questions requiring visual web evidence from domains including finance, biomedicine, and climate science; (2) Evaluate on existing benchmarks augmented with visual subtasks (GAIA-Visual, ChartQA-Web); (3) Ablate the contribution of visual extraction vs. text-only fallback; (4) Compare against GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro as baselines on report generation quality and factual accuracy.

Real-world research requires not just finding information but critically assessing source reliability.

Proposed Method: We propose CriticalThinker, which augments the Think-Search-Draft paradigm with an explicit Source Credibility Evaluation (SCE) module. During web navigation, before incorporating any retrieved content, the model executes a credibility sub-reasoning chain assessing: (1) domain authority signals (publication venue, author credentials, citation counts), (2) temporal validity (publication date vs. claim currency), (3) cross-source consistency via automatic claim triangulation across multiple retrieved documents, and (4) logical coherence with established facts. We train the SCE module using a contrastive DPO approach where preference pairs are constructed by pairing reports citing high-credibility vs. low-credibility sources for identical queries, with human expert annotations on source quality.

Experiments: We construct a benchmark of 500 research queries with deliberately seeded misinformation sources. Evaluation metrics include: factual accuracy of generated reports (verified against gold knowledge bases), source quality scores, and hallucination rates. Baselines include WebThinker, standard RAG pipelines, and GPT-4o with browsing. We also test on GAIA and GPQA to verify no reasoning degradation.

title: MultimodalThinker: Extending Deep Research Agents to Vision-Grounded Web Reasoning with Screenshot-Aware Navigation
description: Problem: WebThinker and similar deep research agents operate primarily on extracted text, discarding rich visual information present on web pages (charts, diagrams, infographics, tables rendered as images). This limits performance on tasks requiring visual evidence synthesis, such as scientific figure interpretation, financial chart analysis, or UI-based navigation where textual extraction fails. Proposed Method: We extend the Think-Search-and-Draft paradigm to incorporate multimodal perception at each web interaction step. Instead of relying solely on text extraction, our agent—MultimodalThinker—captures full-page screenshots and passes them through a vision-language model (VLM) backbone alongside extracted text. A Visual Evidence Extractor module identifies salient visual regions (charts, tables, equations), generates textual descriptions, and stores them in a multimodal scratchpad. We augment the RL-based DPO training with preference pairs contrasting text-only versus vision-augmented reasoning traces, rewarding responses that correctly cite visual evidence. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on visually-rich variants of GAIA and HLE where answers require chart/figure interpretation; (2) Construct a new benchmark, WebVisQA, comprising 500 questions answerable only via visual web content; (3) Ablations comparing text-only extraction vs. screenshot-augmented reasoning; (4) Measure report quality on Glaive with visual figure integration scored by human evaluators.

title: TemporalThinker: Teaching Large Reasoning Models to Reason About Information Freshness and Temporal Uncertainty During Web Research
description: Problem: When LRMs like WebThinker retrieve web information, they treat all retrieved content as equally reliable regardless of temporal provenance. This leads to reasoning failures when sources conflict due to being from different time periods, or when the model must reason about evolving facts (e.g., current stock prices, recent scientific discoveries, ongoing conflicts). The model cannot distinguish stale information from fresh, nor reason about how confident it should be given temporal gaps. Proposed Method: We introduce TemporalThinker, which augments the WebThinker framework with explicit temporal reasoning capabilities. Key contributions include: (1) a Temporal Provenance Tracker that tags retrieved content with publication dates and estimates information decay rates by domain; (2) a Temporal Conflict Resolution module that, when contradictory facts are found, explicitly reasons about which is more recent and whether recency implies correctness; (3) a Temporal Uncertainty Quantification head that outputs calibrated confidence scores based on information age relative to query time; (4) RL training via DPO using synthetic temporal conflict scenarios where ground truth temporal ordering is known. Experiments: We construct TempConflict-QA, a benchmark of 2,000 questions requiring temporal disambiguation across web sources, and evaluate on existing benchmarks stratified by temporal sensitivity. We measure answer accuracy, temporal reasoning coherence, and calibration under temporal uncertainty.
